analysis.one_liner: Taxes billionaires' pandemic wealth gains to cover everyone's out-of-pocket health costs for a year.
analysis.headline: The bill to tax billionaires' pandemic wealth gains at 60% and fund a year of free out-of-pocket health care never received a committee vote or any Senate action before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have imposed a one-time 60% tax on any increase in a billionaire's net worth during the COVID-19 pandemic — measured from March 18 through December 31, 2020, on gains above $1 billion — and used the money to pay all out-of-pocket health costs, including prescription drugs, for every U.S. resident for one year. During that year, insurers could not raise cost-sharing or cut benefits, providers could not bill patients extra, and collection of COVID-related medical debt had to stop. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021. [S1][S2][S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident: for one year, the government would pay all out-of-pocket costs — deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance — for people with public or private insurance, and pay Medicare rates for care given to uninsured people, including COVID-19 testing, treatment, and vaccines. Outpatient prescription drugs would be free for uninsured people. Providers would have to stop all medical debt collection during the year and could never collect COVID-related medical debt afterward. Insurers would be barred from raising cost-sharing or cutting benefits while the program ran. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Imposed a one-time 60% tax on the pandemic wealth gains of people with more than $1 billion in net assets, measured from March 18, 2020 to December 31, 2020.

Had the Department of Health and Human Services pay all out-of-pocket costs — deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance — for insured patients, and pay Medicare rates for care furnished to uninsured patients, for one year, covering COVID-19 testing, treatment, and vaccines as well as other medically necessary care.
Made outpatient prescription drugs free for uninsured people, with manufacturers required to reimburse pharmacies for the difference.
Required providers to halt all medical debt collection during the year and barred any collection of COVID-related medical debt afterward, even for care given before the program.
Barred health plans from raising cost-sharing or cutting benefits during the year, and barred participating providers from balance-billing patients beyond what insurance pays.
Authorized $400 billion to run the program and required weekly public reports on payments and on racial and other disparities in COVID health outcomes.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with more than $1 billion in net assets would pay a one-time 60% tax on their pandemic-era wealth gains above $1 billion, not deductible against income tax. Drug manufacturers would have to reimburse pharmacies for the difference on prescription drugs dispensed free to uninsured people, or lose Medicare drug coverage for their products. [S2][S3]

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to unrealized gains in assets that are hard to value, such as stakes in private companies, and the bill leaves valuation and anti-abuse rules — including rules for trusts — to the Treasury Department, making enforcement difficult for a one-time tax written in months.

Because the tax is on wealth rather than income and applies retroactively to gains accrued since March 2020, it was legally untested and would likely have faced court challenges under the Constitution's limits on direct taxes.
The $400 billion program funding is only an authorization, not an appropriation — Congress would still have had to pass separate legislation to actually provide the money.

The tax could force billionaires to sell assets to pay a bill on paper gains they had not yet converted to cash, which even supporters of taxing wealth might handle differently in a permanent, carefully designed tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits, the bill's costs fall on a very small group — people whose net worth crossed $1 billion or grew during the pandemic — while its benefits are broad: a year in which no one faced a deductible, copayment, surprise bill, or COVID-related medical debt. The honest objections are about design rather than size: a retroactive one-time tax on unrealized, hard-to-value gains is administratively hard to enforce and legally untested, and the $400 billion funding was authorized but not guaranteed. Those are fixable drafting problems, and the bill never received a hearing or markup where they could have been worked out.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee never took the bill up after it was referred there, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill on August 6, 2020, with Gillibrand and Markey as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
The Finance Committee took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its history — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill attracted only two additional cosponsors beyond its three original sponsors in the roughly five months it existed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Billionaires kept 100% of their pandemic-era wealth gains, and drug manufacturers and insurers avoided the reimbursement requirements and benefit-lock rules the bill would have imposed. Patients facing out-of-pocket costs and COVID-related medical debt received no relief from this bill.

industries.industry: Billionaire households (individuals with over $1 billion in net assets)
industries.note: The bill's core funding source: a one-time 60% tax on each billionaire's pandemic-era gains above $1 billion, with anti-abuse rules aimed at trusts and family transfers. This group bears the entire cost of the program.

Manufacturers would have to reimburse pharmacies for the gap between the free drugs dispensed to uninsured people and what the government pays, or lose Medicare coverage for their drugs. The bill directly targets a major revenue channel.

Insurers would be locked into their existing benefit levels and barred from raising cost-sharing for a year — a real constraint — but the government reimburses patients' cost-sharing, so premiums and the insurers' role as the coverage channel remain intact.

Providers get guaranteed payment — Medicare rates for uninsured patients' care and reimbursement of patient cost-sharing — in exchange for agreeing not to bill patients directly or pursue COVID medical debt afterward.
